question: What is the main job of the human immune system?

options.A: Pumping oxygenated blood throughout the body tissues
options.B: Regulating hormone levels in the endocrine glands
options.C: Breaking down dietary fats for energy production
options.D: Distinguishing between self and non-self cells

explanation: Spot on! The immune system's superpower is recognizing what belongs to your body (self) and what is a dangerous stranger (non-self) so it can fight back. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h1)

question: A patient asks why the body gets a fever when fighting an infection. What is the best way to explain this?

options.A: Increased heat directly destroys the nervous system to stop pain signals.
options.B: Fever is a sign that the body is failing to fight off the pathogen.
options.C: Elevated body temperatures help slow down pathogen reproduction and boost immune activity.
options.D: Fever causes blood vessels to constrict and trap the infection in one limb.

explanation: You got it! Think of a fever as turning up the heat to make germs uncomfortable while giving your white blood cells a turbocharged boost. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which type of immunity are you born with that gives you immediate, general protection?
explanation: That's correct! Innate immunity is your body's built-in, ready-to-go security system that protects you from day one without needing prior practice. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h2)

question: What is the main feature that sets adaptive immunity apart from innate immunity?

options.A: Dependence purely on physical barriers like unbroken skin
options.B: Inability to recognize different strains of bacteria
options.C: Development of specific memory cells for future exposures
options.D: Activation only after a person reaches adulthood

explanation: Brilliant! Adaptive immunity remembers past fights, creating memory cells so it can crush the same germ even faster next time. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h2)

question: Where do T lymphocytes mainly go to mature in the human body?
explanation: Spot on! T cells get their start in the bone marrow, but they graduate and mature in the thymus gland (hence the 'T'). [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h3)

question: What is the main job of secondary lymphoid organs like lymph nodes?

options.A: Secreting digestive enzymes into the gastrointestinal tract
options.B: Synthesizing steroid hormones for stress management
options.C: Filtering lymph and housing mature cells to trap pathogens
options.D: Producing red blood cells to carry oxygen to tissues

explanation: Correct! Think of lymph nodes as security checkpoints where immune cells hang out, waiting to trap and filter out invading germs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h3)

question: Which specific cells are responsible for producing and releasing antibodies during an infection?
explanation: You nailed it! When B cells are activated, they transform into plasma cells, which act like tiny antibody factories pumping out weapons against the infection. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h4)

question: What is the purpose of opsonization in the immune response?

options.A: Dissolving the cell walls of healthy human tissues
options.B: Coating a pathogen with antibodies to make phagocytosis easier
options.C: Preventing white blood cells from entering infected areas
options.D: Converting antigens into harmless nutritional vitamins

explanation: That's right! Opsonization is like putting a 'kick me' or 'eat me' sign on a germ by coating it with antibodies so phagocytes can gobble it up easily. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h4)

question: Which chemical is released mainly by mast cells to cause blood vessels to widen during inflammation?
explanation: Spot on! Histamine is the chemical culprit that dilates your blood vessels, causing redness and swelling when your immune system reacts. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h5)

question: Why does a localized area swell up during an acute inflammatory response?

options.A: Fluid and white blood cells leak through permeable capillary walls.
options.B: Excess water is stored in fat cells surrounding the injury site.
options.C: Red blood cells get trapped inside closed lymphatic vessels.
options.D: Local muscles contract violently to push out invading bacteria.

explanation: Correct! When capillary walls become leaky, fluid and helpful white blood cells rush out into the tissues, causing that classic swelling. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of giving a patient a vaccine?

options.A: Stimulating memory cell production without causing severe disease
options.B: Lowering high blood pressure caused by systemic infection
options.C: Killing all normal flora bacteria living in the gut
options.D: Providing immediate short-term relief from chronic joint pain

explanation: Brilliant! Vaccines safely teach your adaptive immune system to recognize a germ and build memory cells without making you really sick. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h6)

question: How does herd immunity help protect vulnerable people in a community?

options.A: Community members take prophylactic antibiotics to sterilize public water supplies.
options.B: High vaccination rates reduce the spread of pathogens, protecting those who cannot be immunized.
options.C: Vaccinated people share their active antibodies directly through casual skin contact.
options.D: Healthy individuals absorb all airborne germs so sick people do not breathe them.

explanation: You got it! When almost everyone is vaccinated, the disease has nowhere to travel, forming a protective shield around those who can't get vaccines. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h6)

question: What do we call it when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own healthy tissues?
explanation: Spot on! 'Auto' means self, so autoimmunity happens when the body's defenses accidentally turn against its own healthy cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of an immunodeficiency disorder?

options.A: Recurrent and unusually severe opportunistic infections
options.B: Prolonged recovery times from minor illnesses
options.C: Enhanced resistance to common environmental pathogens
options.D: Increased vulnerability to unusual fungal or viral agents

explanation: That's right! An immunodeficiency weakens your defenses, so you definitely wouldn't have enhanced resistance to everyday germs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h7)

question: Why might an immunocompromised patient with a serious infection fail to show classic signs like pus?

options.A: They lack sufficient white blood cells to mount a standard inflammatory response.
options.B: Their body temperature is permanently too high to produce visible exudate.
options.C: Strong antibiotics destroy all signs of inflammation before they begin.
options.D: Their skin becomes completely impermeable to bacterial accumulation.

explanation: You nailed it! Pus is mostly a pile-up of dead white blood cells (neutrophils). If the body is low on them, it can't form pus. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h8)

question: A patient on chemotherapy has a very low neutrophil count (400 cells/mm3). What is the most critical nursing action?

options.A: Allow unrestricted visitors to boost the patient's emotional morale.
options.B: Encourage the patient to eat fresh, unwashed salads for vitamins.
options.C: Discontinue all infection monitoring since white blood counts fluctuate.
options.D: Implement protective isolation and enforce strict hand hygiene protocols.

explanation: Brilliant nursing judgment! With a dangerously low neutrophil count, protecting the patient from outside germs through strict isolation and handwashing is top priority. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h8)
